## Batching and Dispatch

### Purpose

The outer batching wrapper (added by Chris Penney) divides subjects into groups for memory management. Without batching, preprocessing (z-score calculation, recentering, reference table merges) for the full dataset must fit in memory at once. For large datasets (100s of thousands or millions of subjects), this can cause memory pressure. The wrapper processes one batch at a time, then combines results.

### Subject-level batching

Batching occurs at the **subject level**, not the row level. All of a given subject's rows — across all parameters (WEIGHTKG, HEIGHTCM, HEADCM) and all ages — are assigned to the same batch. This is a logistical choice: batching by subject before the child/adult age split keeps both halves of a subject's data within the same outer-batch iteration, so output reassembly can combine child and adult results for that subject without cross-batch bookkeeping. The child and adult algorithms themselves are independent and do not share trajectory data across the age split.

### Interaction with the child/adult age split

After batching by subject, `cleangrowth()` splits each batch's data by `adult_cutpoint` (default 20 years, range 18–20) into pediatric (`data.all`) and adult (`data.adult`) subsets. A subject whose rows span the cutpoint will have some rows sent to `cleanchild()` and others to `cleanadult()`. This is intentional: the child and adult algorithms are independent pipelines with no interaction between them. A subject's child measurements are cleaned using only their other child measurements, and their adult measurements are cleaned using only their other adult measurements.

Both sets of rows for such a subject are guaranteed to be in the same batch because batching is done on `subjid` before the age split. The result assembly at the end of each batch iteration recombines the child and adult results for the batch's subjects, and `rbindlist()` combines across batches.

### Two batching systems in the code

The code contains two layered batching systems with different purposes:

**System 1 — Outer wrapper (for memory management):**

- In `child_clean.R`, inside `cleangrowth()`.
- Creates batches of up to `batch_size` subjects (default 5000; configurable via the `batch_size` parameter): `patients[, batch := (seq_len(.N) - 1L) %/% batch_size + 1L]`.
- Iterates the batches with a `for` loop. Each iteration filters the input to the current batch's `subjid` values (both the pediatric `data.all` and the adult `data.adult` are limited to those subjects), runs preprocessing and the child/adult algorithms on just that batch, and pushes the per-batch result onto `results_list`.
- After the loop, `rbindlist(results_list)` combines per-batch results and the merge against `data.batch` restores user input columns.

**System 2 — Inner batching (for parallelism):**

- Also in `child_clean.R`, inside each outer-batch iteration.
- Assigns round-robin batch numbers to subjects in the already-filtered `data.all`: `(seq_along(subjid.unique) - 1L) %% cores + 1L`.
- When `parallel = FALSE` (or a single-core auto-detect), `cores = 1`, making this a no-op: all subjects in the outer batch go to a single `cleanchild()` call.
- When `parallel = TRUE`, dispatches via `foreach::foreach(...) %dopar%` to process inner batches in parallel across CPU cores.

The inner batching subdivides whatever data the outer wrapper provides into parallel work units. With `parallel = FALSE`, it has no effect. The adult algorithm has its own inner parallel batching system, structured identically.

### Parallel processing

`parallel = TRUE` runs the inner batches concurrently. The worker processes are separate R sessions that resolve libraries from `.libPaths()` and need `system.file()` access to the `inst/extdata/` reference tables. This means growthcleanr must be installed (via `devtools::install_github()`, `devtools::install_local()`, or CRAN), not merely source-loaded via `devtools::load_all()`.

**Practical note for developers:** There is a limitation that applies only to package developers. Most uses of `devtools` — including `devtools::install_github("growth-data-tools/growthcleanr", ...)` and `devtools::install_local(".")` — actually **install** the package into your R library, and `parallel = TRUE` works normally after those calls. The issue only appears when a developer uses `devtools::load_all()` to load the source tree into the current R session without installing (a workflow used for rapid iteration on package code). The workaround in that case is to run `devtools::install_local(".")` once, which takes only a few seconds.

Results are bit-identical to sequential processing (verified on the 77,721-row `syngrowth` dataset). Typical observed speedups on 2,697 subjects with many errors (which results in longer run-time): ~114 s at `parallel = FALSE`, ~65 s at `cores = 2` (1.7×), ~30 s at `cores = 4` (3.9×).

Batch-invariant setup (the `exclude.levels` factor and the Tanner velocity reference) is performed once outside the outer loop so the cost is not repeated per batch; the WHO velocity tables are loaded per batch inside `cleanchild()`.

### Partial runs and preloaded references

Two mechanisms support workflows that call growthcleanr many times on overlapping data (simulation loops, error-injection pipelines, secure-environment workflows with updated data extracts): preloaded reference tables, and the `gc_partial_run()` wrapper for incremental re-cleans.

**`ref_tables` + `gc_preload_refs()`.** `gc_preload_refs()` reads the CDC and WHO growth-chart reference files once and returns a named list of closures (`mtz_cdc_prelim` and `mtz_who_prelim`). Passing that list as the `ref_tables` argument to subsequent `cleangrowth()` calls skips the per-call `read_anthro()` disk reads (≈0.9 seconds per call). The return value is a session-lifetime object; rebuild only if the reference files themselves change.

```r
refs <- gc_preload_refs()
res  <- cleangrowth(..., ref_tables = refs)
```

**`gc_partial_run()` — incremental re-cleans.** When you re-clean a dataset that changed for only a subset of subjects, `gc_partial_run()` re-cleans just those subjects and reuses the earlier cleaned result for everyone else. This is correct because growthcleanr cleans each subject independently after reference recentering, so re-cleaning only the changed subjects yields exactly the rows those subjects would get in a full run; the combined result equals `cleangrowth(new_data, ...)`.

```r
baseline <- cleangrowth(old_data)
updated  <- gc_partial_run(new_data, baseline, changed_subjids = who_changed)
```

`gc_partial_run()` is a thin wrapper around `cleangrowth()`, not a mode of it: it slices `new_data` to the changed subjects (plus any subjects newly added relative to the cache; removed subjects are dropped), hands that subset to a single ordinary `cleangrowth()` call, and row-binds the retained cached rows to the fresh rows, ordered by `id`. Everything passed in `...` — including `checkpoint_dir`, `checkpoint_size`, `batch_size`, `ref_tables`, and the output switches — is forwarded verbatim to that inner call, so a large changed subset can still be checkpointed. Because the cache never enters `cleangrowth()`, it cannot interact with the cleaning core.

Requirements: input must be long format; both `new_data` and `cached_output` must carry a per-row unique `id` (the stable key that links retained and fresh rows), and `id` values must be stable across runs; and `...` must specify the same output options used to build `cached_output` — if the resulting columns differ, `gc_partial_run()` stops rather than silently produce `NA`-filled rows. See `?gc_partial_run` for the full contract.

Because only the changed subjects are cleaned, the per-call cost scales with the fraction of subjects that changed: re-cleaning 5 % of subjects does roughly 5 % of the cleaning work of a full run (plus a small fixed cost to slice and merge). The savings are largest in loops where each iteration perturbs only a few subjects.

### Checkpointed runs (the `checkpoint` / `checkpoint_dir` switch)

**How the switch resolves.** The pair `checkpoint` / `checkpoint_dir` is resolved once, before the checkpoint loop, into a concrete target. In priority order: a nested per-checkpoint call (`.checkpoint_driven`) never re-checkpoints; `checkpoint = FALSE` disables checkpointing and, if a `checkpoint_dir` was also passed, ignores it with a warning (the "nothing on disk" escape hatch is absolute); an explicit `checkpoint_dir` is honored as a persistent, resumable location (`keep_checkpoints` as given); and the default `checkpoint = TRUE` with no directory writes to an ephemeral `file.path(tempdir(), "growthcleanr_checkpoints")` with `keep_checkpoints = FALSE` and `checkpoint_resume = FALSE`, engaging **only when the data exceeds one checkpoint** (`uniqueN(subjid) > checkpoint_size`). A single checkpoint is the whole dataset cleaned in one in-memory pass and gives no benefit, so at or below one checkpoint's worth of subjects the run stays fully in memory and writes nothing — which keeps the on-by-default behavior free for small and typical data. On a system whose temp dir is RAM-backed (e.g. Linux `tmpfs`), a very large dataset should pass a `checkpoint_dir` on a real disk. User-facing guidance is in `vignette("large-datasets")`.

Whichever way it engages, the mechanics are the same. `cleangrowth()` splits subjects into checkpoints of `checkpoint_size` (default 5000, capped at 9999 checkpoints — a `checkpoint_size` that would exceed the cap is increased to stay within it, with a warning when you chose the size), cleans each checkpoint, and writes that checkpoint's result to its own `checkpoint_NNNN.rds` file in the checkpoint directory before moving to the next. After the last checkpoint it combines all checkpoint files into a single result in the original input order. Reference tables are preloaded once (via `gc_preload_refs()`) and reused across checkpoints. Because subjects are independent, the checkpointed result is identical to cleaning the whole dataset at once — this includes wide / semi-wide input and output, which reshape once around the checkpoint loop (input is reshaped to long before checkpointing; the combined long result is re-widened once at the end).

Internally each checkpoint is cleaned by a nested `cleangrowth(checkpoint_dir = NULL)` call in long mode: the input funnel, date parsing, and `id` generation happen once in the outer call, so a checkpoint receives canonical long data with a valid unique `id` and every subject's rows land in one checkpoint. Carry-through of extra non-growthcleanr columns works under checkpointing: the parked columns are reattached once to the combined result at the end, so a checkpointed run returns the same columns as a non-checkpointed one. Every subject is cleaned independently, so checkpointing never changes a result. The `adult_cutpoint` (clamped to `[18, 20]`) is finalized once in the outer call and forwarded to each checkpoint so every checkpoint uses the same value; growthcleanr does not change the cutpoint based on the data, so this is a dataset-independent constant. The all-adult advisory (which suggests `adult_cutpoint = 18` when the data looks adult-only) and the consolidated input warning are each emitted once from the outer call over the whole dataset rather than per checkpoint.

`checkpoint_size` is the *persist* unit (one `.rds` per checkpoint) and is independent of `batch_size`, the *in-memory* unit within a checkpoint; `batch_size < checkpoint_size` is allowed, so a checkpoint sized for a reasonable number of resumable files can still be processed in smaller memory batches.

The per-checkpoint files exist for durability and resumability:

- By default (`checkpoint_resume = FALSE`) a run starts fresh: any checkpoint files already in `checkpoint_dir` are deleted at the start, so the combined result contains only the current run's checkpoints and a re-run never silently mixes in stale results from a different prior dataset.
- With `checkpoint_resume = TRUE`, checkpoints that already have a checkpoint file are skipped, so an interrupted run resumes on only the unfinished checkpoints. Checkpoint membership is determined by the sorted set of subjects and `checkpoint_size`, so resuming requires the same dataset and `checkpoint_size`. It also requires the same other `cleangrowth()` arguments; these are not checked, and a mismatch silently mixes results from different settings.
- `keep_checkpoints` (default `TRUE`) governs only whether the files are retained after a successful run; it is independent of `checkpoint_resume`, which governs start-of-run reuse.

`cleangrowth_checkpoint()` is a **deprecated** wrapper that forwards to `cleangrowth(checkpoint_dir = ...)` — its `use_existing_checkpoint_results` argument maps to `checkpoint_resume` — and warns on use; it will be removed in a future version. `cleangrowth_checkpoint_combine()` re-combines the saved checkpoint files without re-running the algorithm — useful if all checkpoints completed but the final combine step failed. It reads every `checkpoint_NNNN.rds` file in the directory. User-facing usage is in `vignette("large-datasets")`.

**Two unrelated uses of "checkpoint."** The `checkpoint_data` capture in Phase 12 of `cleangrowth()` is an internal z-score snapshot merged back onto the output for diagnostics; it is unrelated to `checkpoint_dir` and the checkpointed-run machinery that saves per-checkpoint result files to disk. The shared word is incidental.

### Progress output

`cleangrowth()` reports progress at one of **three levels**, set by the `quietly` and `verbose` flags (both plain and checkpointed `checkpoint_dir` modes):

- **Silent** (`quietly = TRUE`) — nothing is printed: no progress lines and no cleaning summary.
- **Minimal** (the default) — a one-line `cleaning in progress` header (subject / measurement / unit counts), an `X/Y` counter as each memory **batch** or **checkpoint** finishes, and the end-of-run cleaning summary. A single-batch, non-checkpointed run therefore prints just the header and the summary.
- **Verbose** (`verbose = TRUE`, which implies `quietly = FALSE`) — the detailed view: the milestone lines (`preprocessing`, `cleaning child`/`cleaning adult`, the per-batch `BATCH i/n` banner) plus granular per-step diagnostics (pre-filter and iteration counts for CF, EWMA, SDE, Evil twins; adult step headers). Intended for development and debugging.

The three nested processing units keep distinct, fixed names: **checkpoint** (`checkpoint_size`; used whenever a run has more than `checkpoint_size` subjects, unless `checkpoint = FALSE`), **batch** (`batch_size`, the in-memory split inside one `cleangrowth()` call), and parallel group (verbose only).

A **minimal** (default) checkpointed run — header, a per-checkpoint `X/Y` counter, then the summary:

```
[10:22:58] growthcleanr: cleaning in progress: 435,000 subjects, 1,740,000 measurements, 87 checkpoints of up to 5,000 subjects | checkpoint_dir: results/gc_ckpt

==================================================
  CHECKPOINT 1 / 87  |  5,000 subjects
==================================================
[10:23:36] checkpoint 1/87: done | 32s | elapsed 32s
...
[11:09:30] all 87 checkpoints complete | 435,000 subjects, 1,740,000 rows | total 46m32s
************************************************************
growthcleanr cleaning summary  (1,740,000 measurements)
  ...
************************************************************
```

At the **verbose** level each checkpoint additionally prints its `preprocessing` / `cleaning child` / `cleaning adult` milestone lines and the per-step diagnostics. A plain `cleangrowth()` call (no `checkpoint_dir`) prints the same header and summary; when `batch_size` forces more than one memory batch it adds a one-line `batch i/n -- done` counter at the minimal level (and the fuller `BATCH i/n` banner at verbose). Under a checkpointed run, each per-checkpoint `cleangrowth()` call is told its framing is owned by the checkpoint driver, so it stays quiet while the driver supplies the header, the per-checkpoint progress, and the total. When `log_file` is set, the full log is written there even under `quietly = TRUE`, so a colleague can monitor a run remotely.

---

## Data Requirements and Input Format

### Calling styles

`cleangrowth()` supports two calling styles:

1. **Data-frame style (primary).** Pass a `data.frame` or `data.table` as the first argument (`data`). The six per-row arguments (`subjid`, `param`, `agedays`, `sex`, `measurement`, `id`) are then column-name strings, defaulting to the canonical names. Examples:
   ```r
   cleangrowth(df)                                    # all defaults
   cleangrowth(df, subjid = "patid", id = "row_id")   # remap two columns
   ```
2. **Vector style (legacy).** Omit `data`; pass each field as a vector via named args, e.g. `cleangrowth(subjid = df$subjid, param = df$param, ...)`. Retained for backward compatibility.

The data-frame path extracts vectors from `data` and merges into the vector path; both produce identical results.

### Flexible sex and parameter coding

`cleangrowth()` accepts a range of `sex` and `param` codings so data from varied sources needs less pre-formatting, while guarding against silent miscoding. Both interpretations preserve the user's verbatim submission (echoed back in the output `sex` / `param` columns); the interpreted values gc worked with are available as `gc_internal_sex` / `gc_internal_param` under `internal_detail` (or `full_detail`).

**Sex.** By default `0`, `"m"`, `"b"`, `"male"`, `"boy"` are read as male and `1`, `"f"`, `"g"`, `"female"`, `"girl"` as female — matched case-insensitively and whitespace-trimmed. Supply `sex_coding` to use your own codes; it is a named list whose `male` and `female` elements are the code vectors, and it **replaces** the defaults wholesale:

```r
cleangrowth(df, sex_coding = list(male = c(0, "M", "boy"), female = c(1, "F", "girl")))
```

Handling of the interpreted sex:

- **Recognized** codes clean normally.
- **Missing** (`NA`/blank) and **present-but-unrecognized** codes on pediatric rows are set aside as `Exclude-Missing-Info`, contributing an "unrecognized sex" bullet (which names the offending values and leads with the `sex_coding` fix) to the consolidated input warning, so a coding gc did not expect is visible, not silent. Pediatric measurements are cleaned only with a recognized sex value (the child z-scores are sex-specific). If **no** pediatric row has a usable value in the sex column and there are no adult rows, the run stops, since nothing could be cleaned. If there are adult rows, the run continues: the pediatric rows are set aside and the bullet says that this is every pediatric measurement and asks you to check the sex column mapping. In either case, when every pediatric row is at least 18 years old, the message also suggests `adult_cutpoint = 18` so all values are cleaned with the adult algorithm.
- **Adult rows.** A sex column is always required, but the sex column value may be blank or `NA` for adults (ages at or above `adult_cutpoint`): the adult algorithm does not require a valid value in the `sex` column, but when available, it is used in the Evil Twins step and in calculating whether a value falls in the unit error range.
- **The `1`=male/`2`=female trap.** growthcleanr reads `1` as female. A column coded `1`=male/`2`=female would therefore misclassify every male as female while only the `2`s drop out — a plausible-looking wrong answer. So when the default coding is in use and every present sex value is `1` or `2` (with at least one `2`), `cleangrowth()` **hard-stops** and tells the user to recode or to declare the coding with `sex_coding = list(male = 1, female = 2)`. Passing an explicit `sex_coding` suppresses the guard. The guard is checked once on the whole dataset, so under checkpointing it stops before the first checkpoint is cleaned, however the data are sorted. A column with pediatric rows and more than one subject in which every value is `1` has no `0` or `2` to reveal the coding and could be single-sex data under either scheme, so it is not stopped: it is read as female with a prominent warning, which an explicit `sex_coding` also removes.

**Parameter.** growthcleanr recognizes only the spelled-out canonical tokens — `WEIGHTKG`, `WEIGHTLBS`, `HEIGHTCM`, `HEIGHTIN`, `LENGTHCM`, `LENGTHIN`, `HEADCM`, `HEADIN` — matched case-insensitively and whitespace-trimmed. There are deliberately **no built-in abbreviations**: a short label such as `WT`, `HT`, or `HC` is *not* assumed to be a growthcleanr parameter, because it just as easily names something that is not a body measurement (a statistical sample weight, for instance). To have a non-canonical label recognized, declare it with `param_coding`. The imperial tokens convert at 2.54 cm/in (`HEIGHTIN` → `HEIGHTCM`, `LENGTHIN` → `LENGTHCM`, `HEADIN` → `HEADCM`) or 2.2046226 lb/kg (`WEIGHTLBS` → `WEIGHTKG`).

Supply `param_coding` to map your own labels. A remapped label **defaults to its metric target**; to declare that a column is imperial, route it to an imperial parameter:

```r
# route two custom labels; treat a "WEIGHT" column as pounds and "HT"/"STATURE" as cm
cleangrowth(df, param_coding = list(WEIGHTLBS = "WEIGHT", HEIGHTCM = c("HT", "STATURE")))
```

It is a named list keyed by canonical parameter. A name that is not a canonical parameter, or one label mapped to two parameters, is an error. Params matching nothing are set aside as `Exclude-Not-GC-Param` (a bullet in the consolidated input warning, never a stop — extracts legitimately carry labs and vitals).

**Systematic unit-error warning.** After cleaning, if more than 20% of a parameter's cleaned values fall in the unit-error range (`unit_error_range`; magnitudes consistent with a metric/imperial mix-up), `cleangrowth()` emits a soft `warning()` — a large share suggests the whole column is in the wrong unit (e.g. weight recorded in pounds but labeled `WEIGHTKG`, or a column mapped to a metric target that was actually imperial). Fix by labeling the column with the imperial parameter or mapping it via `param_coding`.

### Input format: long, semi-wide, and wide

The `input_format` argument selects the shape of `data`:

- **`"long"` (default)** — one row per measurement, the classic format described above.
- **`"semi_wide"`** — one row per *visit*: a `subjid`, an age source, a `sex`, and one column per parameter (at most one value per parameter per visit).
- **`"wide"`** — one row per *subject*: a `subjid`, a `sex`, and repeated observation blocks marked by a `_N` column suffix (`agedays_1`, `wt_1`, `ht_1`, `agedays_2`, `wt_2`, …).

Semi-wide and wide both require the data-frame style, and both are reshaped to canonical long form *before* any cleaning, so results are identical to submitting the same measurements in long format. Results come back in the same shape by default (`output_format` mirrors `input_format`); see **Output format: semi-wide** and **Output format: wide** below. Set `output_format = "long"` for the full per-measurement result table, which merges back onto the source data by `subjid`/`param`/`agedays`.

The format is never auto-detected: `input_format` defaults to `"long"`, so semi-wide or wide data submitted without setting it is not silently mis-cleaned — it fails, because long format requires `param`/`measurement` columns (and a single `agedays` column) that reshaped data lack. When the columns look reshaped, the error names `input_format` as the likely fix.

Parameter value columns are mapped with `semiwide_cols`, a named list of gc-parameter → column name. If omitted, columns literally named as recognized parameters (`WEIGHTKG`, `HEIGHTCM`, `LENGTHCM`, `HEADCM`, `WEIGHTLBS`, `HEIGHTIN`, `LENGTHIN`, `HEADIN`) are used:

```r
# columns already named WEIGHTKG / HEIGHTCM / HEADCM
cleangrowth(visits, input_format = "semi_wide")

# custom value-column names
cleangrowth(visits, input_format = "semi_wide",
            semiwide_cols = list(WEIGHTKG = "wt_kg", HEIGHTCM = "ht_cm", HEADCM = "head_cm"))
```

Structural columns reuse the usual remap arguments (`subjid`, `sex`, and either an `agedays` column or `dob` + `visit_date` columns, from which `agedays` is computed). Behavior details:

- **Empty cells vs. zeros.** An `NA` cell means "no measurement of that parameter at this visit" and is dropped during reshape (no output row). A literal `0` is **not** an empty cell: exactly as in long format, its value is returned unchanged in `measurement` and the row is flagged `Exclude-Missing-Info` (growthcleanr treats `0` as missing for cleaning purposes but never alters the value it hands back). Do not pad absent measurements with `0` — use an empty/`NA` cell.
- **At least one recognized parameter column** must be present (otherwise an error). A missing weight or height/length column warns; a missing head-circumference column warns only when the data include any visit under 2 years of age.
- **Length vs height is a long-format-only feature.** Semi-wide input always uses default handling of linear measurements (values under 2 years are treated as recumbent length, values 2 years and over as standing height, using estimated corrected age for children whose data are consistent with prematurity or small-for-gestational age (SGA) and who receive an assigned gestational age for cleaning purposes), so `length.adjust = TRUE` is rejected. A `LENGTHCM`/`LENGTHIN` column is accepted at any age and gets default handling, giving the same result as mapping it to `HEIGHTCM`/`HEIGHTIN`; the adult algorithm ignores the length/height label entirely. To use the two-directional `length.adjust` reconciliation, submit the data in long format.
- **Duplicate column names are an error.** If a `subjid`, `sex`, age, or parameter column name appears more than once, growthcleanr stops. R's column indexing silently keeps only the first such column, so cleaning would proceed on a dataset with a shadowed, dropped column — rename or drop the duplicate instead. (An unmapped extra column is simply ignored: parameters come from the column you map, not from any value.)
- **Same-day duplicates.** Because a visit row holds at most one value per parameter, two measurements of the same parameter on the same day must appear as **two rows sharing the same `(subjid, agedays)`**. growthcleanr keeps one and flags the other as a same-day extraneous value, exactly as for long input. Each parameter is handled independently (weight/height pairing across same-day rows is not preserved).
- **Per-measurement ids / same-day tiebreaking.** The reshape mints deterministic per-measurement ids in a stable, documented emission order (subject in first-appearance order; within a subject by visit, then by parameter in weight → height/length → head-circumference order). If you supply an id (the `id` argument, or a column named `id`), a subject's visit rows are ordered by your id first (sorted by value, so character ids sort alphabetically) and by input row second; the id need not be unique. The same input always produces the same result, but *which* of two same-day duplicates is flagged can depend on this emission order. To control same-day tiebreaking, give same-day visit rows ids in the order you want (a higher id is preferred, except at birth), or reformat to long format and set a per-measurement `id` yourself.
- **Ids in long output.** With `output_format = "long"`, each input row becomes one output row per measurement, so a row id cannot identify a single measurement. growthcleanr returns its own per-measurement number as `gc_internal_id`, and your id (the `id` argument, or a column named `id`) under your own column name, repeated on each measurement from that input row. With no id column there is no `id` column in the output. Your other columns are returned too (`carry_through`), repeated on each measurement from their row. A column with your name always holds only your own values: if your id or another column has the name of a column growthcleanr returns (e.g. `exclude` or `param`), it comes back as `userinput_<name>`, with a warning.
- **Column names in long output.** The subject, sex and age columns come back under your own names (e.g. `patid`, `male`, `age_d`; for wide input, the age prefix such as `age`), as in long input. `param` and `measurement` have no column of yours to be named after, so they use those names; on the date route the computed ages are `agedays`.
- **Factor value columns** are taken by their labels (never their level codes), with a warning naming the columns.

### Wide input: the block layout

Wide data has one row per subject and repeats a whole observation across numbered columns. **You choose the prefix; growthcleanr requires the `_N` suffix** and discovers the blocks from it — there is no need to declare how many observations your widest subject has:

```r
# subjid sex agedays_1 wt_1 ht_1 agedays_2 wt_2 ht_2 ...
cleangrowth(subjects, input_format = "wide", output_format = "long",
            wide_cols = list(WEIGHTKG = "wt", HEIGHTCM = "ht", HEADCM = "hc"))
```

`wide_cols` maps each gc parameter to its column-name *prefix*. If omitted, prefixes literally named as recognized parameters are used (`WEIGHTKG_1`, `HEIGHTCM_1`, …). A mapped prefix with no `<prefix>_N` columns in the data is an error, so map only the parameters your dataset actually carries.

- **Levels.** `subjid` and `sex` are patient-level (one unsuffixed column each). The age source is per block: either `agedays_1`, `agedays_2`, … (rename the prefix with `agedays = "age"` if your columns are `age_N`), or — on the date route — a single patient-level `dob` column plus `visit_date_1`, `visit_date_2`, ….
- **Ragged subjects** need no special handling. A subject with 3 observations in a 6-block table simply leaves blocks 4–6 empty; empty cells are dropped during reshape.
- **Block numbers** are any non-negative integers. A `_0` block (some exports number a baseline observation `_0`) is accepted and, like every block, is ordered by its number — so `_0` sorts ahead of `_1`. Block numbering may start at `0` or `1`; a missing intermediate block warns (see Strictness) but does not fail.
- **Empty cells vs. zeros, missing-parameter warnings, and same-day duplicates** behave exactly as for semi-wide input (above). Two blocks carrying the same `agedays` are resolved as same-day extraneous values.
- **A value with no age** — a populated `wt_3` where `agedays_3` is missing — keeps its row and is flagged `Exclude-Missing-Info`, the same as a long-format row with a missing `agedays`.
- **Per-measurement ids** are minted in a stable, documented emission order: subject in first-appearance order; within a subject by input row, then block number ascending; within a block by parameter in weight → height/length → head-circumference order. The same-day tiebreaking caveat above applies. A user `id` column (the `id` argument, or a column named `id`) identifies a row, not a measurement: it does not affect cleaning, comes back unchanged in wide output, and in long output follows the semi-wide rule above (your id under your column name, growthcleanr's number in `gc_internal_id`).
- **Strictness** — these warn rather than fail, and the data are processed as submitted:
  - a gap in the block numbering (`ht_1`, `ht_3`, no `ht_2`);
  - more blocks than `max_blocks` (default 25) — raise it, or reshape to long or semi-wide for data this wide. An implausible block count errors instead, since it usually means the `_N` suffixes parsed wrong;
  - ages that do not increase across ascending blocks;
  - a `subjid` appearing on more than one row (each row's blocks become additional observations for that subject).
- **Errors:** two parameters mapped to the same prefix; a duplicate structural column name (two `subjid` columns); two columns landing on the same block — an exact duplicate name, or leading-zero padding (`ht_1` and `ht_01`), including duplicated age or visit-date columns; no age source; `length.adjust = TRUE` (length vs height is a long-format-only feature — see the semi-wide behavior notes above).

Wide input returns wide output by default (see **Output format: wide** below); set `output_format = "long"` for the per-measurement table.

### Output format: semi-wide

With `output_format = "semi_wide"` (the default for semi-wide input), growthcleanr returns **your table**: every column you submitted, unchanged, one row per input row, with the requested growthcleanr columns inserted immediately to the right of the value column they describe.

```r
cleangrowth(visits, input_format = "semi_wide")
```

```
subjid agedays sex  wt_kg  exclude_wt_kg  ht_cm  exclude_ht_cm  site
A      100     0    6.0    Include        60.0   Include        clinic1
```

- **Which columns are added** is controlled by `widened_emit`, default `"exclude"`. Any per-measurement output column may be named — `"bin_exclude"`, `"exclude_detailed"`, `"unit_error_range"`, `"measurement"`, `"agedays"`, and so on. Naming a column whose own switch was not enabled (e.g. `"exclude_detailed"` without `exclude_detail = TRUE`) is an error. Note that semi-wide output does **not** inherit the long-format defaults: `bin_exclude` and `unit_error_range` appear only if you ask for them.
- **Naming.** growthcleanr's own output columns take the value-column suffix only (`exclude_wt_kg`, `bin_exclude_wt_kg`). growthcleanr's *internal version of a value you supplied* takes a `gc_internal_` prefix (`gc_internal_meas_wt_lbs`, `gc_internal_param_wt_lbs`, `gc_internal_agedays`), because those report what growthcleanr used rather than what you submitted.
- **Your values are never rewritten.** Submit weights in pounds and the `wt_lbs` column comes back in pounds. `widened_emit = "measurement"` adds `gc_internal_meas_<column>` with the value growthcleanr worked from (converted to metric; `length.adjust` does not apply to semi-wide or wide input), and automatically adds `gc_internal_param_<column>` alongside it so the units of that value are visible in the data rather than only in this vignette.
- **Empty cells** get an `NA` verdict: a visit with no head-circumference measurement has `NA` in `exclude_head_cm`. A visit row where every parameter is empty is still returned.
- **Same-day duplicates** stay on their own visit rows, each with its own verdict — the round-trip is keyed by input row, not by `(subjid, agedays)`.
- **Other columns.** With `carry_through = TRUE` (default) every column you submitted returns. `carry_through = FALSE` returns only the structural columns (`subjid`, `sex`, the age source), the parameter value columns, and the growthcleanr columns.
- **Not available for:** long input (growthcleanr cannot infer visit rows from long data — same-day measurements are ambiguous; reshape the long output yourself with `data.table::dcast()`). Checkpointed runs *are* supported (the re-widen happens once around the checkpoint loop).

### Output format: wide

With `output_format = "wide"` (the default for wide input), growthcleanr returns your subject rows the same way — every submitted column unchanged, one row per subject, with each verdict column slotted immediately right of the value block column it describes:

```r
cleangrowth(subjects, input_format = "wide",
            wide_cols = list(WEIGHTKG = "wt", HEIGHTCM = "ht"))
```

```
subjid sex agedays_1 wt_1 exclude_wt_1 ht_1 exclude_ht_1 agedays_2 wt_2 exclude_wt_2 ...
A      0   100       6.0  Include      60.0 Include      200       8.0  Include      ...
```

Everything from **Output format: semi-wide** carries over — the same `widened_emit` control, the same naming (`exclude_wt_1`, `gc_internal_meas_wt_1`), values never rewritten, empty ragged blocks getting `NA` verdicts, `carry_through`, and the direct echo of your input table (so rows can't be lost or reordered and ragged blocks come back exactly as submitted). Two wide-specific points:

- **`agedays` widens per block, not per row.** `widened_emit = "agedays"` adds `gc_internal_agedays_1`, `gc_internal_agedays_2`, … — one per block, because the age varies within a subject row. `subjid` and `sex` stay one unsuffixed column each. Each carries the whole-day age growthcleanr cleaned on; on the date route this is the only way to see the ages growthcleanr computed.
- **Not available for:** long or semi-wide input (growthcleanr will not invent observation blocks from data that is not already wide). Checkpointed runs *are* supported. Wide input with `output_format = "long"` gives the full per-measurement table instead.

### Required input fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `subjid` | any | Subject identifier (default column name: `"subjid"`) |
| `param` | character | `"WEIGHTKG"`, `"WEIGHTLBS"`, `"HEIGHTCM"`, `"HEIGHTIN"`, `"LENGTHCM"`, `"LENGTHIN"`, `"HEADCM"`, or `"HEADIN"` |
| `agedays` | numeric | Age in days at measurement |
| `sex` | any | By default `0`/`m`/`b`/`male`/`boy` = male and `1`/`f`/`g`/`female`/`girl` = female (case-insensitive); see `sex_coding` |
| `measurement` | numeric | Recorded value in units specified by `param` |
| `id` | numeric or character (optional) | Unique row identifier. If omitted (no `id` column in data-frame style, or NULL in vector style), a warning is issued and sequential integers `1:N` are auto-generated. |

### Input handling

- `measurement == 0` is replaced with `NaN` (treated as missing) in the internal variable `v`
- Imperial measurements are converted to metric before processing: HEIGHTIN multiplied by 2.54 and relabeled HEIGHTCM; WEIGHTLBS divided by 2.2046226 and relabeled WEIGHTKG
- LENGTHCM is relabeled to HEIGHTCM. By default (`length.adjust = FALSE`) no length-height correction is applied (except for gestational-age-corrected children between chronological age 2 and corrected age 2; Phase 8, fact 6), because of variability in measurement and recording practices across health systems; see [Phase 8: Length vs. height handling](#phase-8-lengthcm-heightcm-relabel) for the optional reconciliation.
- `sex` is recoded to integer: 0 = male, 1 = female
- Cleaning uses the whole-day value of `agedays` (`floor(agedays)`, as on the date route, so a negative fractional age such as -0.5 is day -1 and is set aside like other negative ages); the submitted value, fractional or not, is what the output `agedays` column returns
- Data are split by `adult_cutpoint` (default 20 years): rows with `agedays < cutpoint * 365.25` go to the child algorithm; rows at or above go to the adult algorithm

### Sorting

The primary sort order is:

```
setkey(data.df, subjid, param, agedays, internal_id)
```

This sort is critical for deterministic results. `internal_id` (assigned 1:N in `id` order at entry) breaks ties when multiple measurements share the same `subjid`, `param`, and `agedays` (same-day duplicates). If `internal_id` is not included in the sort key, SDE resolution order is undefined and results may differ between sequential and parallel runs.

### Internal identifiers

- `line` — row number in original input order; used to restore output order
- `index` — sequential row number after sorting; used as internal key within `cleanchild()`
- `id` — user-provided or auto-generated; returned in output only. `internal_id` is the tiebreaker in sorting and SDE resolution
- `v` — working measurement value (metric, with 0 → NaN)
- `v.orig` — copy of `v` before any transformations

### Trying a sample first (`gc_runtrial()`)

Before committing to a full run, `gc_runtrial()` lets you confirm your data are formatted correctly and that growthcleanr is reading your columns, sex coding, and parameters the way you intend. It draws a small sample of patients, runs `cleangrowth()` on them with the *exact* configuration you pass through (`...`), and prints a short diagnostic report: how the input was interpreted (format, column mapping, age range), dedicated **SEX** and **PARAMETERS** sections (the two highest-risk settings) that each show what values map to each category, any present-but-unrecognized values, and the resulting counts, then anything flagged while reading and a summary of the cleaning result. The cleaned sample is returned invisibly, with the structured diagnostic attached as `attr(x, "gc_trial")`.

```r
gc_runtrial(mydata)                                  # 100 random patients, default long
gc_runtrial(mydata, n = 50, seed = 1,                # reproducible 50-patient sample
            input_format = "semi_wide")
```

- **Sampling is by patient** — all of a sampled subject's rows are kept, so trajectories stay intact. `sampling = "random"` (default) with an optional `seed` for reproducibility, or `sampling = "first"` for the first `n` subjects. Random is effectively free: the cost is running growthcleanr on the sampled patients, the same either way.
- **Data-frame style only**, and the trial always analyses/returns results in long format so the diagnostic is well defined regardless of `output_format`.
- **A configuration hard-stop is reported, not re-thrown.** If the setup makes `cleangrowth()` stop (a forgotten `input_format`, a sex coding it will not guess), the trial surfaces that stop as the headline finding with the same guidance the error carries — turning a hard error into setup help. This makes it a natural engine for a "preview my setup" step in a wrapping app.

## Z-Score Infrastructure

The child algorithm computes and uses multiple z-score variants. Understanding which is used where is essential for debugging. The adult algorithm does not use WHO/CDC z-scores; it works with raw measurements and BMI, plus a small embedded NHANES CSD reference used only in Evil Twins and the unit-error range.

### Calculation method: CSD (Conditional Standard Deviation)

All z-scores in the cleaning algorithm use the CSD method, the same approach the CDC uses for its modified z-scores (Kuczmarski et al., 2002; full citation in `vignette("algorithm-functions")`):

```
If measurement < M:  sd = (measurement - M) / csd_neg
If measurement >= M: sd = (measurement - M) / csd_pos
```

Where:

- `M` = age/sex-specific median from reference table
- `csd_pos` = half the distance from M to the value at z = +2, precomputed in reference tables
- `csd_neg` = half the distance from M to the value at z = -2, precomputed in reference tables

This is NOT the standard LMS z-score used in clinical practice. CSD z-scores are intentionally more sensitive to extreme high values for weight, which helps the algorithm detect implausible measurements.

### Reference tables

| Table file | Source | Used for |
|------------|--------|----------|
| `growthfile_who.csv.gz` | [WHO 2006](https://www.who.int/tools/child-growth-standards) | HT/WT age < 5y; all HEADCM |
| `growthfile_cdc_ext_infants.csv.gz` | [CDC 2000](https://www.cdc.gov/growthcharts/) (weight, height, head circumference); CDC 2022 extended BMI charts (Wei et al., 2020) (BMI) | HT/WT age ≥ 2y |
| `fent_foraga.csv.gz` | Fenton 2025 | Approximated Fenton median weights by gestational age, used for weight → estimated gestational age; see [Gestational-age reference values](#ga-reference-values) |
| `fenton2025_ms_lookup_smoothed.csv` | Fenton 2025 | Approximated Fenton CSD values (M, S_upper, S_lower) for CSD z-scores; see [Gestational-age reference values](#ga-reference-values) |
| `rcfile-resmoothed.csv.gz` | Derived | Recentering medians |

### Z-score variants

| Variable | Source | Description |
|----------|--------|-------------|
| `sd.orig_who` | WHO CSD | WHO-only CSD z-score |
| `sd.orig_cdc` | CDC CSD | CDC-only CSD z-score |
| `sd.orig` | Blended | Age-blended WHO/CDC CSD z-score (see below); not replaced by GA correction (which writes `sd.corr`), except that Child Step 2b rescores default GA-window height rows 0.7 cm lower (Phase 8, fact 6); also the uncorrected score used in CF rescue (Child Step 6) and PIV (Child Step 7) |
| `sd.corr` | GA-corrected | Gestational-age-corrected z-score for potcorr subjects; equals `sd.orig` for others |
| `tbc.sd` | Recentered | `sd.orig - rcmedian.sd`; primary score used by most algorithm steps |
| `ctbc.sd` | Recentered corrected | `sd.corr - rcmedian.sd`; used alongside `tbc.sd` in Evil Twins and EWMA steps |


### Age blending — main z-score (`sd.orig`)


| Age range | Parameter | Formula |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| < 2 years | any | `sd.orig = sd.orig_who` |
| 2–5 years | HT, WT | `(sd.orig_cdc × (age-2) + sd.orig_who × (5-age)) / 3` |
| > 5 years | HT, WT | `sd.orig = sd.orig_cdc` |
| any age | HEADCM | `sd.orig = sd.orig_who` |

Note: The blending window is 2–5 years with divisor 3. At exactly 2 years, the formula yields 100% WHO. At exactly 5 years, it yields 100% CDC.

***Code-verified detail:*** The code assigns WHO for `ageyears < 2` and CDC for `ageyears > 5` (strict inequality). For ages exactly 2.0 or 5.0, the smooth_val condition (`>= 2 & <= 5`) applies, so they go through the blending formula. This means ages exactly at the boundaries use the blending formula, which gives 100% WHO at 2.0 and 100% CDC at 5.0.

### Age blending — corrected z-score (`sd.corr`)

For potcorr subjects, `sd.corr` is calculated in two stages:

**Stage 1 — Compute `sd.c` (the corrected z-score before smoothing into original):**

First, corrected WHO and CDC z-scores (`sd.c_who`, `sd.c_cdc`) are calculated using corrected age (`cagedays`) with an adjustment for standing vs. recumbent position when chronological age is 730 days or more but corrected age is under 730 days (+0.7 cm for both WHO and CDC; see [Phase 8, fact 6](#phase-8-lengthcm-heightcm-relabel)).

Then `sd.c` is assigned using WHO/CDC blending with the same 2–5 year window as `sd.orig`:

- HEADCM: WHO at all ages
- HT/WT age ≤ 2: WHO
- HT/WT age 2–5: weighted blend `(who × (5-age) + cdc × (age-2)) / 3`
- HT/WT age ≥ 5: CDC

Then the gestational-age reference z-score is preferred over corrected WHO for ages ≤ 2: if it (`unmod_zscore`) is available, it overwrites `sd.c`; corrected WHO is used only as fallback.

**Stage 2 — Smoothing corrected into original:**

| Age range | Formula |
|-----------|---------|
| ≤ 2 years (potcorr) | `sd.corr = sd.c` (fully corrected) |
| 2–4 years | `(sd.orig × (4 - age) + sd.c × (age - 2)) / 2` |
| > 4 years | `sd.corr = sd.orig` (no correction) |

Note: This smoothing window is 2–4 years with divisor 2, which is narrower than the main WHO/CDC blending window (2–5 years, divisor 3).

### Age blending — `calc_and_recenter_z_scores()` (Child Step 15/16 p_plus / p_minus)

This helper function, used in the Child Step 15/16 pre-loop (EWMA2 / moderate trajectory outliers), recalculates recentered z-scores for each row's perturbed `p_plus` and `p_minus` measurement values. It uses the same WHO/CDC blending formula as the main z-score calculation (2–5 year window) so that the perturbed z-scores are on the same footing as `tbc.sd`.

| Age range | Parameter | Formula |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| < 2 years | any | WHO only |
| 2–5 years | HT, WT | `(cdc × (age-2) + who × (5-age)) / 3` |
| > 5 years | HT, WT | CDC only |
| any age | HEADCM | WHO only |

### Recentering

After z-score calculation, the algorithm subtracts age-, sex-, and parameter-specific median z-scores to produce tbc.sd:

```
tbc.sd = sd.orig - rcmedian.sd
ctbc.sd = sd.corr - rcmedian.sd
```

Recentering uses a precomputed reference file (`inst/extdata/rcfile-resmoothed.csv.gz`) whose medians were built offline by smoothing per-day median SD scores from large EHR samples (see `vignette("recentering")` for the derivation). Callers can override by passing a `sd.recenter` data.table or data.frame to `cleangrowth()`.

The recentering median file is indexed by param, sex, and agedays. It is merged into the data by an exact join on these keys.

**Required schema for a custom `sd.recenter` table.** A user-supplied override must be a data.table or data.frame (converted to a data.table) with these columns:

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `param` | character | `"WEIGHTKG"`, `"HEIGHTCM"`, or `"HEADCM"` |
| `sex` | integer | 0 (male) or 1 (female) |
| `agedays` | integer | Age in whole days; the join matches each row's exact `agedays` |
| `rcmedian.sd` | numeric | Population median (in CSD z-score units) to subtract from `sd.orig` / `sd.corr` |

A median column named `sd.median` is also accepted. growthcleanr works on a copy of the supplied table (the caller's object is not keyed or renamed) and sets the key itself. The table must have exactly one row per `param`, `sex`, and `agedays` (duplicates stop with an error), and a median for every `param`, `sex`, and `agedays` of the child measurements to be cleaned, meaning every child row that is not already set aside (missing or unusable values) and is not head circumference at 5 years or older. Adult rows are not recentered. If any such row has no median (including an `NA` median), `cleangrowth()` stops before cleaning, reports how many measurements are uncovered, and lists up to five example param/sex/agedays combinations. Anything other than `NA` or a table (for example a character string) also stops with an error.

**Recentering limitation.** Recentering has a small but sometimes meaningful impact on cleaning results. The provided recentering data are based on growth from a single large health system. Some datasets may have different growth patterns. Users may wish to use their own data to create a recentering reference. If doing so, we would suggest creating smoothed medians using data from your own study population or a similar population, and would caution about bias related to small sample sizes and overfitting.

## Cross-Algorithm Differences

The two algorithms differ in many cross-cutting respects that are worth understanding when reading either codebase or when combining results.

| Aspect | Child algorithm | Adult algorithm |
|--------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Data structure | Single `data.df` data.table; rows are never physically removed | Copies rows into separate working dataframes (`h_subj_df`, `w_subj_df`) that shrink as values are excluded |
| Exclusion mechanism | Set `exclude` column; filter with `.child_valid()` | Remove from working dataframe |
| Output column | `exclude` | `result` (mapped to `exclude` by `cleangrowth()` in Phase 14) |
| `Exclude-Missing` assignment | Pre-dispatch in `cleangrowth()` | Post-dispatch in `cleangrowth()` |
| Z-scores | CSD z-scores (WHO/CDC blend) | No WHO/CDC z-scores — raw measurements (BMI computed internally for some thresholds); small NHANES CSD reference in Evil Twins and the unit-error range |
| Param scope | HT, WT, HC | HT, WT only (no HC) |
| Rounding tolerance | None | 0.12 cm/kg on all threshold comparisons |
| SDE tiebreaking at birth | Lowest `internal_id` (pre-postnatal shift) | N/A (no births) — keeps highest `internal_id`, except identical same-day duplicates keep lowest |
| Permissiveness levels | Not implemented | 4 levels: loosest/looser/tighter/tightest |
| Iteration exponent (EWMA) | Age-dependent: -1.5 at ≤1 y, -3.5 at ≥3 y, linear between | -5 |
| `perclimit` scope | N/A | Adult Step 11Wa: subject-level max wt; Adult Step 11Wb: observation-level |
| Reference data | WHO 2006, CDC 2000 and CDC 2022 extended BMI, approximated Fenton (2025) values for GA correction | No WHO/CDC references; small embedded NHANES CSD constants (Evil Twins, unit-error range) |
| Adult-specific output cols | NA on child rows | `mean_ht`, `bin_result` |
| Child-specific output cols | `cf_rescued`, `sd.orig*`, `sd.corr`, `tbc.sd`, `ctbc.sd` | NA on adult rows |
| Sort key (within algorithm) | `setkey(data.df, subjid, param, agedays, internal_id)` | All sorts include `internal_id` (integer) as final tiebreaker; `as.character(internal_id)` used for named-vector keys |
| Missing-as-infinity edge handling | N/A | `ifelse(is.na(...), Inf, ...)` for edge EWMA values |

For the full child working-dataframe mechanics (how `.child_valid()` works, the temp-SDE soft-flag mechanism, SDE-Identical removal during CF detection), see `vignette("child-algorithm")` → Working Dataframe and Output.

## Variable Glossary (wrapper-level)

For child-specific variables (CF working columns, EWMA working columns, exclusion/status columns), see `vignette("child-algorithm")` → Variable Glossary.

### Input and identification

| Variable | Type | Created | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `line` | integer | Preprocessing | Original row number; used to restore output order |
| `id` | any (optional) | Input | User-provided row identifier. Fully optional: when absent / `NULL` / contains `NA` / non-unique, a warning is issued and sequential `1:N` ids (in input row order) are auto-generated for internal use. The user's original `id` (whatever was supplied — even if invalid) is restored to the output `id` column at Phase 15 trim. The gc-used id is exposed as the optional `gc_internal_id` column when `display_gc_id = TRUE` (or `full_detail = TRUE`). Not used as a tiebreaker by the algorithm — `internal_id` is. |
| `internal_id` | integer | `cleangrowth()` | Sequential integer `1:N` assigned in id-sorted order at session start. Used throughout as the final sort-tiebreaker and for named-vector indexing where applicable (age-dependent tiebreaking keeps the lowest `internal_id` at `agedays == 0`, the highest at `agedays > 0`). |
| `index` | integer | `cleanchild` | Sequential `1:.N` within each outer-batch dataframe, reassigned at the top of `cleanchild()` so merges and subset operations within the batch have contiguous keys. |
| `subjid` | any | Input | Subject identifier (any type; preserved as-is into output). |
| `param` | character | Input (post-conversion) | `"WEIGHTKG"`, `"HEIGHTCM"`, or `"HEADCM"` after imperial→metric relabeling. |
| `agedays` | integer | Input | Age in days at the measurement. |
| `sex` | integer | Input | 0 = male, 1 = female. |
| `v` | numeric | Preprocessing | Working measurement value (metric; 0 → NaN). |
| `v.orig` | numeric | Child Step 5 | Copy of `v` captured at the start of Child Step 5, used in Child Step 6 CF detection. |

### Z-score variables

| Variable | Type | Created | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `sd.orig_who` | numeric | Preprocessing | WHO-only CSD z-score |
| `sd.orig_cdc` | numeric | Preprocessing | CDC-only CSD z-score |
| `sd.orig` | numeric | Preprocessing | Blended WHO/CDC CSD z-score (also the uncorrected score used by CF rescue and PIV) |
| `sd.corr` | numeric | Child Step 2b | GA-corrected CSD z-score |
| `rcmedian.sd` | numeric | Recentering | Population median z-score for recentering |
| `tbc.sd` | numeric | Recentering | Recentered blended z-score (`sd.orig - rcmedian.sd`) |
| `ctbc.sd` | numeric | Recentering | Recentered corrected z-score (`sd.corr - rcmedian.sd`) |

### Prematurity correction variables

| Variable | Type | Created | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `potcorr` | logical | Child Step 2b | TRUE if subject may need GA correction (subject-level) |
| `potcorr_wt` | logical | Child Step 2b | TRUE for the qualifying first weight row (row-level) |
| `uncorr` | integer | Child Step 2b | 1 if the GA correction was reverted because prematurity was uncorroborated (no consistent early weight and no low same-day height/HC within 3.5 z of the weight); see Phase 4 |
| `fengadays` | numeric | Child Step 2b | Estimated gestational age in days (from the gestational-age reference) |
| `pmagedays` | numeric | Child Step 2b | Post-menstrual age in days |
| `cagedays` | numeric | Child Step 2b | Corrected age in days |

## Output Format

`cleangrowth()` returns a data.table with the following columns by default:

> **Output fidelity.** The echoed input columns (`id`, `subjid`, `param`, `agedays`, `sex`, `measurement`) carry the user's **verbatim submission** — gc never silently alters or drops an input value. Where gc must reinterpret a value internally (imperial → metric, `LENGTHCM` → `HEIGHTCM`, `sex` → `0`/`1`/`NA`, `measurement` `0` → `NaN`), that interpretation is surfaced only in the optional `gc_internal_*` columns (`internal_detail` / `debug`), never in these columns. Full contract: `vignette("output")` §1.

| Column | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `id` | original | User-provided row identifier, preserved as-is (any type). If the user supplied invalid `id` (absent / `NULL` / `NA` / non-unique), `id` here is still the user's original — gc auto-regenerated `1:N` internally but restored the user's input to this column at trim. The gc-used id is exposed as `gc_internal_id` when `display_gc_id = TRUE`. |
| `subjid` | as supplied | Subject identifier, returned in the user's original type (factored internally for grouping, restored verbatim at output). |
| `param` | as supplied | The growth parameter **exactly as submitted** — imperial and `LENGTHCM` labels come back unchanged, not relabeled. gc's internal canonical token is `gc_internal_param` (`internal_detail`). |
| `agedays` | as supplied | Age in days **exactly as submitted** (a fractional age comes back fractional). The whole-day age gc cleaned on is `gc_internal_agedays` (`internal_detail`). With `age_source = "dates"` and an age column present, the age column is returned as submitted and the computed ages as `gc_internal_agedays`, always. |
| `sex` | as supplied | Sex **exactly as submitted** (the verbatim value, e.g. `0`/`1`, `"m"`/`"M"`, or an uninterpretable code). gc's coerced integer (0 = male, 1 = female, else `NA`) is `gc_internal_sex` (`internal_detail`, `debug`, or `full_detail`). |
| `measurement` | as supplied | The measurement value **exactly as submitted** — a submitted `0` returns as `0` (not `NaN`), imperial units are not converted, and a text or factor column keeps its type and values (kept as `meas_input` when the input is text or a factor). gc's internal working value (metric; `0` → `NaN`) is `gc_internal_meas` (`internal_detail`). |
| `exclude` | factor | **Summary** exclusion code or `"Include"` (14 consolidated codes; see `vignette("exclusion-codes")`) |
| `bin_exclude` | character | `"Include"` or `"Exclude"` |
| `unit_error_range` | logical | Informational: `TRUE` when a value's magnitude is consistent with a metric/imperial unit-conversion error AND it is outside the plausible z = −3..+3 band; `FALSE` for the non-evaluable codes (`Exclude-Missing-Info`, `Exclude-Not-GC-Param`, `Exclude-HC-Out-of-Range`). Never affects `exclude` and is not in `exclude.levels`. **Present by default** (`unit_error_range = TRUE`); omit with `unit_error_range = FALSE`. Child zn3/zp3 from `child_z3_reference.csv.gz`; adult from a sex-specific embedded NHANES CSD reference whose missing-sex (`NA`) rows resolve to an M/F-averaged fallback. |
| `mean_ht` | numeric | Returned when the data has adult rows (`mean_ht = FALSE` omits; `TRUE` always returns). Adult height rows only; `NA` elsewhere. See `vignette("output")`. |

**Column naming:** The six data columns (`id`, `subjid`, `param`, `agedays`, `sex`, `measurement`) are renamed in the output to match the user's original argument expressions when those resolve to a simple name. For example, `cleangrowth(subjid = dt$patid, ...)` returns a column named `patid`; `cleangrowth(measurement = dt$v, ...)` returns a column named `v`. Complex expressions fall back to the canonical name.

Further columns are included when the corresponding parameter is set:

| Column | Argument | Description |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| `exclude_detailed` | `exclude_detail = TRUE` | **Detailed** exclusion code or `"Include"`: step-level, keeps the `-C-`/`-A-` prefix, folds RV/`-All`/iteration, renames `PIV`→`Hard-Limit`. Every Detailed code maps to one Summary `exclude` code (see `vignette("exclusion-codes")`). |
| `tri_exclude` | `tri_exclude = TRUE` | `"Include"`, `"Same-Day"` (SDE codes), or `"Exclude"` |
| `cf_status` | `cf_detail = TRUE` | Every row labeled: `"Orig"` (CF-string originator), `"CF-R"` (carried forward and rescued (not excluded as CF); a later step may still exclude it), `"CF-NR"` (excluded CF, rescue-eligible but failed threshold), `"CF-E"` (same-day-extraneous CF -- a CF on a day that also has an Include; never rescue-eligible, never participates in positional string detection; in `cf_rescue = "all"`, same-day CFs are not excluded at this step and are labelled `CF-R`, with `cf_deltaz` NA; Child Step 13 then chooses one value for the day, so such a row can end as `Exclude-Extraneous`), `"Not-CF"` (no CF relationship), or `"Adult"` (adult row) |
| `cf_deltaz` | `cf_detail = TRUE` | Absolute z-score difference (`|sd.orig - originator_z|`) from CF originator for positionally-detected CF candidates; `NA` for Orig, Not-CF, CF-E, and Adult rows. The whole string is decided on its last carried-forward value; values shown on earlier rows are informational. |
| `cf_nextz` | `cf_detail = TRUE` | Signed z-score change (`next sd.orig - this sd.orig`) from a CF row to the next non-CF Included value within (subjid, param), at the time of Step 6 (temp same-day-extraneous rows do not count). Populated for CF-R and CF-NR; `NA` for Orig, Not-CF, CF-E, Adult, and end-of-series cases. The whole string is decided on its last carried-forward value; values shown on earlier rows are informational. |
| `imperial` | `cf_detail = TRUE` | Design aid. Row-level whole/half imperial-unit flag (whole pounds for WEIGHTKG, whole/half inches for HEIGHTCM/HEADCM, tol 0.01 imperial unit), computed from `v.orig` for every row; `NA` on missing-measurement rows (`v.orig` is `NaN`) and Adult rows |
| `cf_dage_orig` | `cf_detail = TRUE` | Design aid. Day gap from a CF row's originator to the CF row (`agedays_CF - agedays_orig`; always positive); populated for CF-R/CF-NR (not same-day CFs in `cf_rescue = "all"`, which are labelled `CF-R` but have `NA`), `NA` otherwise |
| `cf_dage_next` | `cf_detail = TRUE` | Design aid. Agedays analogue of `cf_nextz`: day gap from a CF row (CF-R/CF-NR) to the next eligible non-CF Included value (`agedays_next - agedays_CF`; always positive); `NA` for Orig, Not-CF, CF-E, Adult, and end-of-series cases |
| `corr_val`, `corr_pt` | `corr_detail = TRUE` | Correction-status labels: `corr_val` per value (`"Corrected"` when its GA-corrected z differs from uncorrected, else `"Uncorrected"`; `"Adult"` for adult rows); `corr_pt` per subject (`"Corrected"` if any value is). |
| `tbc.sd`, `ctbc.sd`, `rcmedian.sd` | `recenter_detail = TRUE` | Recentered CSD z-scores (`tbc.sd`, `ctbc.sd`) plus the recentering median subtracted (`rcmedian.sd`). Specialized output for a related tool in development (see `vignette("output")` §5b). Child rows only (`NA` on adult). |
| `sd.orig`, `sd.corr`, `tbc.sd`, `ctbc.sd`, `tbc.p_plus`, `tbc.p_minus`, `ctbc.p_plus`, `ctbc.p_minus` | `debug = TRUE` | Intermediate CSD z-scores (raw + recentered, uncorrected + GA-corrected) plus the ±5%/±1 cm plus/minus perturbation recentered z-scores. Threshold-refinement only; child rows only (`NA` on adult). |
| `gc_internal_id` | `display_gc_id = TRUE` | The id growthcleanr actually used internally: equals the user's `id` when it was valid (no regen), or the auto-regen `1:N` (in input row order) when `id` was absent / `NA` / non-unique. Lets callers recover a reliable per-row key when their input `id` had problems (the `id` column always preserves whatever the user supplied). |
| all of the above | `full_detail = TRUE` | Convenience switch: enables `exclude_detail` + `cf_detail` + `corr_detail` + `recenter_detail` + `debug` + `tri_exclude` + `display_gc_id` + `internal_detail` + `mean_ht` together (not `qm_detail`). |

Internal working columns (`line`, `sd.orig*`, `tbc.sd`, `ctbc.sd`, `cf_rescued`, `bin_result`, checkpoint columns) are used during processing but dropped before the final return. See Phases 14–15 above for where the trim occurs.

For the **child-specific exclusion code list**, see `vignette("child-algorithm")` → Output Format.

For the **adult-specific exclusion code list**, see `vignette("adult-algorithm")`.

## Configurable Arguments (wrapper-level)

The arguments in the table below are used in the wrapper code. Some of these are child- or adult-specific but are handled in the wrapper.

The output-detail switches that add optional columns (`exclude_detail`, `internal_detail`, `qm_detail`, and the ones listed below — `cf_detail`, `corr_detail`, `recenter_detail`, `debug`, `full_detail`, `tri_exclude`, `display_gc_id`, `unit_error_range`) are catalogued in full — with the exact columns each adds — in `vignette("output")`, the single source of truth for the return-value contract.

For arguments used only in the child algorithm code (PIV cutoffs, CF rescue modes, EWMA window, error load, etc.), see `vignette("child-algorithm")` → Configurable Arguments.

For arguments used only in the adult algorithm code (permissiveness presets, wtallow/ET caps, `mod_ewma_f`, `ht_band`, etc.), see `vignette("adult-algorithm")` (and the `adult_permissiveness` / `adult_scale_max_lbs` rows below for the wrapper-level adult arguments).

| Argument | Default | Used in | Description |
|-----------|---------|---------|-------------|
| `id` | NULL | Preprocessing | Optional row identifier. Can be any type (numeric, character, UUID). When absent / `NULL` / `NA` / non-unique, a warning fires and sequential `1:N` ids are auto-generated for internal use; the user's original `id` is preserved in the output `id` column. See `display_gc_id` for surfacing the gc-used id as `gc_internal_id`. |
| `input_format` | `"long"` | Input dispatch (`reshape_adapters.R`) | Shape of `data`: `"long"` (one row per measurement), `"semi_wide"` (one row per visit, one column per parameter), or `"wide"` (one row per subject, repeated `_N` observation blocks). Non-long input is reshaped to long before cleaning and requires the data-frame style. See **Input format: long, semi-wide, and wide** above. |
| `output_format` | NULL | Output | Shape of the returned results; `NULL` mirrors `input_format`. `"long"`, `"semi_wide"`, and `"wide"` are supported. Re-widened output requires the matching input format (checkpointed runs are supported). See **Output format: semi-wide** / **Output format: wide** above. |
| `semiwide_cols` | NULL | `.gc_semiwide_to_long` (`reshape_adapters.R`) | Named list/vector mapping gc parameters to their value columns for semi-wide input, e.g. `list(WEIGHTKG = "wt_kg", HEIGHTCM = "ht_cm", HEADCM = "head_cm")`. `NULL` uses columns literally named as recognized parameters. Only used when `input_format = "semi_wide"`. |
| `wide_cols` | NULL | `.gc_wide_to_long` (`reshape_adapters.R`) | Named list/vector mapping gc parameters to their column-name *prefixes* for wide input, e.g. `list(WEIGHTKG = "wt", HEIGHTCM = "ht", HEADCM = "hc")` for `wt_1`, `wt_2`, `ht_1`, …. `NULL` uses prefixes literally named as recognized parameters (`WEIGHTKG_1`, …). A mapped prefix with no `<prefix>_N` columns is an error. Only used when `input_format = "wide"`. |
| `max_blocks` | 25 | `.gc_wide_to_long` (`reshape_adapters.R`) | Highest number of wide observation blocks expected. More than this warns and still processes every block; an implausible count errors (the `_N` suffixes likely parsed wrong). Only used when `input_format = "wide"`. |
| `dob` | NULL | Preprocessing (age) | Date-of-birth column name (data-frame style only). Column is class `Date` or a text date; a subject with more than one distinct dob value is set aside as `Exclude-Missing-Info`, with a warning. Supplied together with `visit_date` to compute `agedays` as `floor(visit_date - dob)` in whole days. Text dates parse under one of several **order-free** formats — year-first numeric (`2013-03-04`, `2013/03/04`, `2013.03.04`, `20130304`) or English spelled-month (`03mar2013`, `15 Mar 2013`, `March 15, 2024`) — or, for ambiguous numeric day/month dates (`3/4/2013`), only when `date_order` is set. All dates in `dob` and `visit_date` must share one format; the year must be four digits in 1900–2099 (two-digit years rejected). Blank/`NA` and text with no digits (e.g. `"N/A"`) yield a missing `agedays`; a few values that are not real dates are set aside, more than a few stop the run; numeric date integers are rejected. Default `NULL`. See `vignette("wrapper")` §"Date parsing" and `date_order`. |
| `visit_date` | NULL | Preprocessing (age) | Visit (measurement) date column name (data-frame style only). Class `Date` or a text date in the same accepted formats as `dob`. Supplied together with `dob`; see `dob`. Default `NULL`. |
| `age_source` | NULL | Preprocessing (age) | Which age source to resolve `agedays` from: `"agedays"` (the `agedays` column) or `"dates"` (`dob` + `visit_date`). `NULL` auto-resolves — an `agedays` column is used whenever present, otherwise the dates. Set `"dates"` to force date-based ages even when an `agedays` column is also present; that column is then returned as submitted and the computed ages as `gc_internal_agedays`. |
| `date_order` | NULL | Preprocessing (age) | Day-vs-month order for ambiguous numeric `dob`/`visit_date` values (data-frame style only), e.g. `"3/4/2013"`. `"dmy"` reads day-month-year; `"mdy"` reads month-day-year; applied uniformly to the whole run. `NULL` (default) accepts only the order-free formats (year-first numeric and English spelled-month) and errors on numeric day/month dates, so an ambiguous order is never guessed. growthcleanr never auto-detects the order. |
| `carry_through` | TRUE | Preprocessing; output | Data-frame style only. If `TRUE` (default), any column in `data` that is not a resolved role column (`subjid`/`param`/`agedays`/`sex`/`measurement`/`id`) is parked and returned appended after the gc output columns, in original input order and values (`dob`/`visit_date` are echoed back this way). A carried column whose name matches a column gc returns in this run (for example `exclude`, when re-cleaning growthcleanr output) is returned under the name `userinput_<name>`, with a warning; the check uses `.gc_added_output_cols()`, the same list that builds the output trim, so a name gc does not return in this run is left alone. `FALSE` restores the prior drop-all-non-role-columns behavior. With semi-wide or wide output your columns return structurally (the submitted table is the output base), so `TRUE` keeps every column and `FALSE` keeps only the role, id and value columns. For cross-format output (semi-wide or wide input → long output) the adapters return each measurement's input row (`src_row`) and the columns they used (`used_cols`); every other column (incl. `dob`/`visit_date` in semi-wide and `dob` in wide, but not wide per-block columns) is repeated on each measurement from its row, with the same `userinput_<name>` rule, checked before cleaning. |
| `adult_cutpoint` | 20 | Preprocessing | Age (years) dividing the pediatric and adult paths. Subjects with measurements spanning the cutpoint have their pediatric and adult rows cleaned by separate algorithms. |
| `sd.recenter` | NA | Preprocessing (recentering) | `NA` uses the built-in rcfile; `"none"` turns recentering off (`tbc.sd = sd.orig`); a data.table or data.frame (columns `param`, `sex`, `agedays`, `rcmedian.sd`) supplies custom recentering medians, which must cover every param, sex, and agedays of the child measurements to be cleaned, or `cleangrowth()` stops. See `vignette("recentering")`. |
| `length.adjust` | FALSE | Preprocessing (Phase 8, before z-scores) | If `TRUE`, reconciles recumbent-length vs standing-height against what the reference expects, in both directions (±0.7 cm at the 2-year boundary; pediatric-only; **long input only**). Also decides how gestational-age-corrected children between chronological age 2 and corrected age 2 are handled (Phase 8, fact 6). Full rules: the Phase 8 section above (Length vs. height handling). |
| `ref.data.path` | `""` | Preprocessing | Directory override for reference files (CDC/WHO z-score tables, rcfile, velocity tables; the Fenton gestational-age tables are always read from the installed package). Default empty string means use the installed package's `inst/extdata/`. |
| `batch_size` | 5000 | Batching (outer wrapper) | Number of subjects per outer-wrapper batch. Subjects are never split across batches. |
| `parallel` | FALSE | Batching (inner) | If `TRUE`, inner batches dispatch via `foreach::foreach(...) %dopar%` for concurrent processing. Requires the package to be installed (not just `load_all()`-ed). |
| `cores` | NULL | Batching (inner) | Number of parallel workers (= inner batches) when `parallel = TRUE`. `NULL` auto-detects `min(8, detectCores() - 1)` (capped at 8); a whole-number override is respected. Ignored when `parallel = FALSE` (acts as 1). |
| `log.path` | NA | Batching (inner) | Deprecated (warns when supplied); use `log_file`. If non-NA and `parallel = TRUE`, each worker sinks messages to `{log.path}/cleangrowth-{date}-batch-{n}.log`. |
| `ref_tables` | NULL | Performance | Pre-loaded reference closures from `gc_preload_refs()`. Skips repeated disk reads across many `cleangrowth()` calls; see "Partial runs and preloaded references" above. (Incremental re-cleans are a separate wrapper, `gc_partial_run()`, not a `cleangrowth()` parameter.) |
| `tri_exclude` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, adds a `tri_exclude` column with a three-level summary (`Include` / `Same-Day` / `Exclude`). Convenience for downstream filtering. |
| `cf_detail` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, adds the six CF diagnostic columns (`cf_status`, `cf_deltaz`, `cf_nextz`, plus the design aids `imperial`, `cf_dage_orig`, `cf_dage_next`); see the Output Format table and `vignette("cf-rescue")`. |
| `corr_detail` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, adds `corr_val` (per-value) and `corr_pt` (per-subject) GA-correction-status columns. |
| `recenter_detail` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, adds the recentered CSD z-score columns `tbc.sd`, `ctbc.sd`, and `rcmedian.sd` (a subset of the `debug` z-scores); specialized output for a related tool in development (see `vignette("output")` §5b). Child rows only. |
| `debug` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, retains intermediate z-score diagnostic columns (raw/recentered, uncorrected/corrected, plus the plus/minus perturbation z-scores) instead of trimming them, and adds `gc_internal_sex` for all rows. Threshold-refinement only; the z-scores are for child rows only. |
| `full_detail` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, enables `exclude_detail` + `cf_detail` + `corr_detail` + `recenter_detail` + `debug` + `tri_exclude` + `display_gc_id` + `internal_detail` + `mean_ht` together (not `qm_detail`). |
| `unit_error_range` | TRUE | Output | If `TRUE` (default), adds the informational `unit_error_range` logical column (metric/imperial unit-error magnitude flag; never affects `exclude`). Set `FALSE` to omit. |
| `mean_ht` | returned when the data has adult rows | Output | `TRUE` always returns the `mean_ht` column; `FALSE` omits it. |
| `display_gc_id` | FALSE | Output | If `TRUE`, adds a `gc_internal_id` column equal to the id growthcleanr actually used internally — the user's `id` when it was valid, or the auto-regen `1:N` when the user's `id` was absent / `NA` / non-unique and gc had to regenerate. Lets callers recover a reliable per-row key when their input `id` had problems (output `id` always preserves whatever the user supplied). Auto-set `TRUE` by `full_detail`. |
| `quietly` | FALSE | All | Default prints the minimal view (run header, X/Y progress counter, cleaning summary); `TRUE` turns off progress lines and the summary (warnings still appear). The milestone view is `verbose = TRUE`. See **Progress output** below. |
| `verbose` | FALSE | All | When `TRUE`, adds the granular per-step diagnostics (CF / EWMA / SDE / Evil-twins pre-filter and iteration counts, adult step headers) on top of the milestone view. Implies `quietly = FALSE`. Intended for development/debugging. |
| `adult_permissiveness` | `"looser"` | Adult dispatch | Permissiveness preset passed to `cleanadult()`. See Section 1D of `vignette("configuration")` (levels) and `vignette("adult-algorithm")` (settings). |
| `adult_scale_max_lbs` | `Inf` | Adult dispatch | Physical scale upper limit in lbs; passed to `cleanadult()`. |
| `adult_overrides` | `NULL` | Adult dispatch | Optional named list overriding individual adult permissiveness settings (see `vignette("configuration")` Section 1D); spliced into the `cleanadult()` call. |
